claims.claim: Wolfe says an intelligent reader can tell who spoke from what was said, without a speech tag.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Lawrence Person, Nova Express vol. 5 no. 1, Fall/Winter 1998
claims.quote: knows who said that from what was said

claims.claim: Wolfe states that once a person inside the story tells the story, that narrator is necessarily unreliable.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Lawrence Person, Nova Express, Fall/Winter 1998
claims.quote: then the narrator is damn well going to be unreliable
claims.page: answer on The Fifth Head of Cerberus

claims.claim: Wolfe grounds narrator unreliability in courtroom testimony, where several witnesses all trying to tell the truth have nonetheless seen different things.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Lawrence Person, Nova Express, Fall/Winter 1998
claims.quote: all trying to tell the truth, but they have all seen
claims.page: answer on The Fifth Head of Cerberus

claims.claim: Wolfe says a complex story has to be told in a clear structure, because otherwise it is not complex but merely confused.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Lawrence Person, Nova Express, Fall/Winter 1998
claims.quote: or it isn't complex, it's simply confused

claims.claim: The interviewer characterises The Book of the Long Sun as told in a straightforward and transparent narrative style despite its complexity, and Wolfe does not dispute the description.
claims.source: Lawrence Person, question put to Gene Wolfe in Nova Express vol. 5 no. 1, Fall/Winter 1998
claims.quote: told in a very straightforward and transparent narrative style

claims.claim: Wolfe says he began the Sun books with the deliberate decision not to coin invented proper names.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Lawrence Person, Nova Express, Fall/Winter 1998
claims.quote: the idea of not coining Tars Tarkas type names

claims.claim: Wolfe says the right choice for those books was archaic real names and archaic terms rather than coinages.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Lawrence Person, Nova Express, Fall/Winter 1998
claims.quote: using archaic names and archaic terms for things

claims.claim: Wolfe attaches a condition to his use of archaic terms: they must appear in contexts that make their meaning clear to the reader.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Lawrence Person, Nova Express, Fall/Winter 1998
claims.quote: it will be clear to the reader what is meant

claims.claim: Wolfe describes his method of sourcing vocabulary as looking up the Latin or Greek word for what he needs and then finding an English word someone had already anglicised from it.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Lawrence Person, Nova Express, Fall/Winter 1998
claims.quote: someone will have anglicized this term as a new word

claims.claim: Wolfe praises Avram Davidson for building imaginary countries out of obsolete real place names.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Lawrence Person, Nova Express, Fall/Winter 1998

claims.claim: Wolfe describes Davidson's place-naming procedure as taking a third-century name and asking what if this place had survived under that name.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Lawrence Person, Nova Express, Fall/Winter 1998
claims.quote: Suppose this place survived as an entity with that name

claims.claim: Wolfe argues that a very large city would show great diversity across its neighbourhoods and social levels, and calls the monocultured world of much science fiction laziness.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Lawrence Person, Nova Express, Fall/Winter 1998
claims.quote: diversity among the neighborhoods and social levels

claims.claim: Wolfe observes that in a real city people on different social levels already talk in ways that are almost different languages.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Lawrence Person, Nova Express, Fall/Winter 1998
claims.quote: people are talking in ways that are almost different languages

claims.claim: Wolfe says real people are unreliable narrators all the time even when they are trying to be reliable.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, quoted in Wikipedia's Gene Wolfe article, citing Lawrence Person's Nova Express interview (Fall/Winter 1998)
claims.quote: Real people really are unreliable narrators all the time

claims.claim: In the appendix to The Shadow of the Torturer Wolfe states that he could have used invented terms but in no case did so.
claims.source: Wikipedia relaying Gene Wolfe's appendix to The Shadow of the Torturer (cited as Shadow and Claw, Tor 1994, p. 211)
claims.quote: in no case have I done so
